headline: Hitler's Eagle's Nest burned. Nobody was hurt.
summary: Fire took hold of the Kehlsteinhaus, the mountaintop house built for Hitler above Berchtesgaden in Bavaria, at 9:15 on Friday night. Some 200 firefighters fought it on steep ground and it was still burning on Saturday morning. Nobody was hurt. Police are holding a 33-year-old German man while they investigate. Local media say it is largely destroyed.

cover_question.q: Why keep Hitler's house at all?

cover_answer: As a warning. That is what its own website says.
table_question: Keep a bad man's house so people remember, or tear it down?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: You might hear that an old house on a mountain in Germany burned down. It was built long ago for Hitler, a leader who did terrible things, and people kept it so nobody would forget. The fire was high up, like a bonfire on a mountaintop, and firefighters climbed to it all night. Nobody was hurt. The grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: If it comes up at all, the fire on the mountain is the picture and nobody hurt is the ending.
5-7.why_long: A seven-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole thing, and "Hitler" is a word they may have heard with fear in it, so the script makes the fire the picture, a bonfire on a mountain, and keeps Hitler to one plain clause. Cantor found this age is frightened by what it can see, not by history. Expect "was anyone in it?" No. Nobody was hurt.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: Hitler's mountaintop house in Germany survived the war and stayed open as an inn and, its website says, a warning about the Nazis. 200 firefighters climbed up on Friday night, but the slope was too steep, and it burned into Saturday. Police hold a man, 33. It was kept the way you keep a scar.
8-12.why: Built, survived, kept as a warning, burned. The scar is the mechanism.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out why rules and places exist, so the script runs the chain: built for Hitler, survived the war, kept as an inn and a warning, burned on Friday. The scar is the mechanism, a mark kept so you remember. Expect "why would anyone burn it?" Police are holding a man and haven't said. Resist guessing for them.

13-17.script: Should a Hitler house exist at all? Germany kept the Eagle's Nest for 80 years as an inn and, its website says, a warning about the Nazi dictatorship. On Friday night it burned; police hold a man, 33. Second: if someone burned it on purpose, is that vandalism or an argument? Where's your line?
13-17.why: A Nazi building and a warning about Nazis, the same building. Then their line.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things: a building made for Hitler is gone, and so is a place that taught people what he did. The script asks whether such a house should exist, then whether burning it is vandalism or an argument. Kuhn's finding is that they learn to argue by arguing with someone honest. Expect "what would you do with it?" Answer it.

5-7.a: A leader in Germany long ago who started a war and had millions of people killed. He lost. People kept his old house so nobody forgets.

8-12.q: Why keep Hitler's house at all?
8-12.a: As an inn and a warning. Its own website says so.

8-12.q: Did the man do it on purpose?
8-12.a: Police don't know yet. They're holding a man, 33, while they check.

13-17.a: Nobody has said. Local media say it is largely destroyed.

13-17.q: Isn't it good that it's gone?
13-17.a: Some will say so. It was a lesson site. Ask what that is for first.
